# Project Logbook: Population Spike Map of Australia

## Background

This project adapts and extends [Milos Popovic’s](https://github.com/milos-agathon "Milos Popovic’s GitHub") technique for making 3D population spike maps using rayshader in R. The original work focused on relatively compact regions which are densly populated across their landmass (e.g., parts of Europe), whereas this attempt seeks to apply the method to the entire Australian continent using the Kontur Population dataset.

```{r}
#######################################################
#                 Making crisp spike maps with R
#                 Milos Popovic
#                 2023/03/12
########################################################
# install rayshader & rayrender from the source
# devtools::install_github("tylermorganwall/rayshader")
# devtools::install_github("tylermorganwall/rayrender")

# libraries we need
libs <- c(
    "tidyverse", "R.utils",
    "httr", "sf", "stars",
    "rayshader"
)

# install missing libraries
installed_libs <- libs %in% rownames(installed.packages())
if (any(installed_libs == F)) {
    install.packages(libs[!installed_libs])
}

# load libraries
invisible(lapply(libs, library, character.only = T))

### 1. DOWNLOAD & UNZIP DATA
### ------------------------
url <-
    "https://geodata-eu-central-1-kontur-public.s3.amazonaws.com/kontur_datasets/kontur_population_DE_20220630.gpkg.gz"
file_name <- "germany-population.gpkg.gz"

get_population_data <- function() {
    res <- httr::GET(
        url,
        write_disk(file_name),
        progress()
    )

    R.utils::gunzip(file_name, remove = F)
}

get_population_data()

### 2. LOAD DATA
### -------------
load_file_name <- gsub(".gz", "", file_name)

# Lambert projection 
# might not be the best solution for non-European countries
# if it creates a skewed map, please use:
# crsLONGLAT <- "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0"

crsLAEA <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=52 +lon_0=10 +x_0=4321000 +y_0=3210000 +datum=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"
get_population_data <- function() {
    pop_df <- sf::st_read(
        load_file_name
    ) |>
        sf::st_transform(crs = crsLAEA)
}

pop_sf <- get_population_data()

head(pop_sf)
ggplot() +
    geom_sf(
        data = pop_sf,
        color = "grey10", fill = "grey10"
    )

### 3. SHP TO RASTER
### ----------------

bb <- sf::st_bbox(pop_sf)

get_raster_size <- function() {
    height <- sf::st_distance(
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymax"]]))
    )
    width <- sf::st_distance(
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymin"]]))
    )

    if (height > width) {
        height_ratio <- 1
        width_ratio <- width / height
    } else {
        width_ratio <- 1
        height_ratio <- height / width
    }

    return(list(width_ratio, height_ratio))
}
width_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[1]]
height_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[2]]

size <- 3000
width <- round((size * width_ratio), 0)
height <- round((size * height_ratio), 0)

get_population_raster <- function() {
    pop_rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
        pop_sf |>
            dplyr::select(population, geom),
        nx = width, ny = height
    )

    return(pop_rast)
}

pop_rast <- get_population_raster()
plot(pop_rast)

pop_mat <- pop_rast |>
    as("Raster") |>
    rayshader::raster_to_matrix()

cols <- rev(c(
    "#0b1354", "#283680",
    "#6853a9", "#c863b3"
))

texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(cols)(256)

# Create the initial 3D object
pop_mat |>
    rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
    rayshader::plot_3d(
        heightmap = pop_mat,
        solid = F,
        soliddepth = 0,
        zscale = 15,
        shadowdepth = 0,
        shadow_darkness = .95,
        windowsize = c(800, 800),
        phi = 65,
        zoom = .65,
        theta = -30,
        background = "white"
    )

# Use this to adjust the view after building the window object
rayshader::render_camera(phi = 75, zoom = .7, theta = 0)

rayshader::render_highquality(
    filename = "germany_population_2022.png",
    preview = T,
    light = T,
    lightdirection = 225,
    lightaltitude = 60,
    lightintensity = 400,
    interactive = F,
    width = width, height = height
)
```

**Australia poses unique challenges:**

-   Massive area with uneven population distribution

-   Dominated by low-density or uninhabited zones

-   Coastal bias in population makes central alignment tricky

-   Projection, masking, and zscale tuning require finesse

## Minimal Refactoring Approach

```{r}
# Setup: libraries, file paths, and projection — same as Section 1

get_population_data <- function() {
    pop_df <- sf::st_read(file_path) |>
        sf::st_transform(crs = crsAU)
    
    return(pop_df)
}

pop_sf <- get_population_data()

# Define file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/01-population-spike-map-AU_raw-population-points.png"

# Save the plot
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pop_sf, color = "grey10", fill = "grey10") +
  theme_void() +  # or theme_classic() if you want axes
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )

ggsave(filename = output_file, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

### 3. SHP TO RASTER
### ----------------

bb <- sf::st_bbox(pop_sf)

get_raster_size <- function() {
    height <- sf::st_distance(
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymax"]]))
    )
    width <- sf::st_distance(
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymin"]]))
    )

    if (height > width) {
        height_ratio <- 1
        width_ratio <- width / height
    } else {
        width_ratio <- 1
        height_ratio <- height / width
    }

    return(list(width_ratio, height_ratio))
}
width_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[1]]
height_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[2]]

size <- 3000
width <- round((size * width_ratio), 0)
height <- round((size * height_ratio), 0)

get_population_raster <- function() {
    pop_rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
        pop_sf |>
            dplyr::select(population, geom),
        nx = width, ny = height
    )

    return(pop_rast)
}

pop_rast <- get_population_raster()

# Define output filename
output_file <- "outputs/images/01-population-spike-map-AU_raw-population-raster-preview.png"

# Open PNG device
png(filename = output_file, width = 2000, height = 1500, res = 300)

# Plot the raster
plot(pop_rast, main = "Population Raster", axes = FALSE, box = FALSE)

# Close the device
dev.off()


pop_mat <- pop_rast |>
    as("Raster") |>
    rayshader::raster_to_matrix()

# Australian-themed colors
cols <- rev(c(
    "#00843D", "#FFCD00", 
    "#FF8000", "#FF4500"
))

texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(cols)(256)

# Create the initial 3D object
pop_mat |>
    rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
    rayshader::plot_3d(
        heightmap = pop_mat,
        solid = F,
        soliddepth = 0,
        zscale = 15,
        shadowdepth = 0,
        shadow_darkness = .95,
        windowsize = c(800, 800),
        phi = 65,
        zoom = .65,
        theta = -30,
        background = "white"
    )

# Use this to adjust the view after building the window object
rayshader::render_camera(phi = 75, zoom = .7, theta = 0)

# Define the output file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/01-population-spike-map-AU.png"

# Render the high-quality image
rayshader::render_highquality(
  filename = output_file,

  interactive = FALSE,
  width = width,
  height = height

```

The above code adapts Milos Popovic's workflow with minimal refactoring to work with Australian Kontour population data. The following changes were made:

-   The data source was switched to a local GPKG file containing Australia's 2023 population grid.

-   The projection was updated to an Australia-appropriate Lambert Conformal Conic (EPSG: 3577–like definition).

-   File saving operations were redirected to an organized `outputs/images/` directory.

-   Plotting functions were adjusted to save copies to the output directory and clean up their appearance.

-   Slightly different colour palette was used, for a bit of Australian flair.

The plots below are from raw sf geometries and raster previews to the final 3D spike map. These help visualise what the code is doing and identify pain points before tackling more advanced effects like landmasks or overlays.

![Figure: Initial geometry plot of Kontur population tiles (unprojected)](images/01-population-spike-map-AU_raw-population-points.png)

The plot above confirms that spatial features were read correctly from the GPKG file and displays expected shapes across Australia.

![Figure: Rasterized population data](images/01-population-spike-map-AU_raw-population-raster-preview.png)

The population `sf` geometry is then converted into a raster grid, suitable for matrix transformation in `rayshader`. Most grid cells contain low population counts, which creates a compressed contrast range across the image. High-density areas such as Melbourne, Sydney, and the east coast are more visibly distinct, but much of inland Australia appears near-empty, making the map look visually flat at this stage. This skewed distribution will need to be addressed when adjusting the colour scale or z-scaling in 3D later.

### Minimum Refactoring Render

![Population Spike Map of Australia](images/01-population-spike-map-AU.png){fig-alt="Version 1"}

The spike map generated by minimal refactoring shows defined peaks along the coastline, but large areas of empty space and no separation of the continent from the oceans, making it hard to identify the Australian landmass. The rayshader `plot_3d()` and `render_highquality()` functions were applied directly to the rasterized population matrix, without adding a landmask or ocean overlay, and the population data was used directly without transformations.

**Limitations:**

-   The map lacks geographic context — no visible coastlines or landforms — which may reduce interpretability for people not familiar with Australian geography.

-   The uniform grey background, while clean, doesn't distinguish ocean from unpopulated land.

-   Difficulty with picking an appropriate `zscale` value to balance visibility of urban spikes against rural areas. High zscale values flatten the map, leaving rural areas nearly invisible, while low values exaggerate urban spikes to the point of obscuring smaller towns.

**Next Steps:**

-   Experiment with different population transformations (e.g., log, square root, power) to enhance visibility of smaller towns and cities.

-   Experiment with transforming the colour matrix to improve visibility of mid size towns and rural areas.

-   Add state boundaries to allow for mapping of population by state.

-   Refactor the code to use functions for a more modular pipeline that can be looped over different transformations, and state boundaries.

-   Overlay geographic features (e.g. coastlines, state borders) to increase readability without clutter.

## Population Transformation

The population data for Australia has a highly skewed distribution, with a few large cities dominating the population counts. This results in a spike map that, while visually striking, lacks depth and variation across the landscape. The initial map, shown above, highlights major urban areas but fails to represent smaller towns and rural regions effectively. Adjusting the `zscale` value alone does not resolve this issue, as it either flattens the map too much or exaggerates the urban spikes to the point where smaller towns are nearly invisible. A quick solution is to experiment with applying log, square root, and power transformations to the population matrix.

The refactored code is below:

```{r}
# Setup: libraries, file paths, and projection — same as Section 1

get_population_data <- function() {
    pop_df <- sf::st_read(file_path) |>
        sf::st_transform(crs = crsAU)
    
    return(pop_df)
}

pop_sf <- get_population_data()

# Define file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/02-population-spike-map-AU_raw-population-points.png"

head(pop_sf)

# Save the plot
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pop_sf, color = "grey10", fill = "grey10") +
  theme_void() +  # or theme_classic() if you want axes
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )

ggsave(filename = output_file, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

### 3. SHP TO RASTER
### ----------------

bb <- sf::st_bbox(pop_sf)

get_raster_size <- function() {
    height <- sf::st_distance(
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymax"]]))
    )
    width <- sf::st_distance(
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
        sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymin"]]))
    )

    if (height > width) {
        height_ratio <- 1
        width_ratio <- width / height
    } else {
        width_ratio <- 1
        height_ratio <- height / width
    }

    return(list(width_ratio, height_ratio))
}
width_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[1]]
height_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[2]]

size <- 3000
width <- round((size * width_ratio), 0)
height <- round((size * height_ratio), 0)

get_population_raster <- function() {
    pop_rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
        pop_sf |>
            dplyr::select(population, geom),
        nx = width, ny = height
    )

    return(pop_rast)
}

pop_rast <- get_population_raster()

# Define output filename
output_file <- "outputs/images/02-population-spike-map-AU_raw-population-raster-preview.png"

# Open PNG device
png(filename = output_file, width = 2000, height = 1500, res = 300)

# Plot the raster
plot(pop_rast, main = "Population Raster", axes = FALSE, box = FALSE)

# Close the device
dev.off()

# Convert the stars object to a matrix for rayshader
pop_mat <- pop_rast |>
    as("Raster") |>
    rayshader::raster_to_matrix()

# Australian-themed colors
cols <- rev(c(
    "#00843D", "#FFCD00", 
    "#FF8000", "#FF4500"
))

texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(cols)(256)

# Alternate colour palette for the texture
# texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(viridisLite::turbo(256))(256)  # alternative color palette

#######################################################
# We will experiment with two transformations for the 
# population data, a square root and a power transformation.
# This should help us to enhance the visibility of smaller
# cities and towns. 
########################################################

# 1. Log transformation
pop_mat_log <- log(pop_mat + 1) # Adding 1 to avoid log(0)

# Check the distribution of values to determine a reasonable Z scale
summary(as.vector(pop_mat_log))

# Create the initial 3D object using the transformed matrix
pop_mat_log |>
    rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
    rayshader::plot_3d(
        heightmap = pop_mat_log,
        solid = F,
        soliddepth = 0,
        zscale = 0.25,  # We need to play with this value with the transformed data
        shadowdepth = 0,
        shadow_darkness = .95,
        windowsize = c(800, 800),
        phi = 65,
        zoom = .65,
        theta = -30,
        background = "white"
    )

# Use this to adjust the view after building the window object
rayshader::render_camera(phi = 75, zoom = .7, theta = 0)

# Define the output file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/02-population-spike-map-AU-log.png"

# Render the high-quality image
rayshader::render_highquality(
  filename = output_file,
  preview = TRUE,
  light = TRUE,
  lightdirection = 225,
  lightaltitude = 60,
  lightintensity = 400,
  interactive = FALSE,
  width = width,
  height = height
)

# 2. Square root transformation
pop_mat_sqrt <- sqrt(pop_mat) 

# Check the distribution of values to determine a reasonable Z scale
summary(as.vector(pop_mat_sqrt))

# Create the initial 3D object using the transformed matrix
pop_mat_sqrt |>
    rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
    rayshader::plot_3d(
        heightmap = pop_mat_sqrt,
        solid = F,
        soliddepth = 0,
        zscale = 0.25,  # We need to play with this value with the transformed data
        shadowdepth = 0,
        shadow_darkness = .95,
        windowsize = c(800, 800),
        phi = 65,
        zoom = .65,
        theta = -30,
        background = "white"
    )

# Use this to adjust the view after building the window object
rayshader::render_camera(phi = 75, zoom = .7, theta = 0)

# Define the output file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/02-population-spike-map-AU-sqrt.png"

# Render the high-quality image
rayshader::render_highquality(
  filename = output_file,
  preview = TRUE,
  light = TRUE,
  lightdirection = 225,
  lightaltitude = 60,
  lightintensity = 400,
  interactive = FALSE,
  width = width,
  height = height
)

# 3. Power transformation
pop_mat_power <- pop_mat^0.7 # Adjust the exponent as needed 0.7 seems to work well

# Check the distribution of values to determine a reasonable Z scale
summary(as.vector(pop_mat_power))

# Create the initial 3D object using the transformed matrix
pop_mat_power |>
    rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
    rayshader::plot_3d(
        heightmap = pop_mat_power,
        solid = F,
        soliddepth = 0,
        zscale = 0.25,  # We need to play with this value with the transformed data
        shadowdepth = 0,
        shadow_darkness = .95,
        windowsize = c(800, 800),
        phi = 65,
        zoom = .65,
        theta = -30,
        background = "white"
    )

# Use this to adjust the view after building the window object
rayshader::render_camera(phi = 75, zoom = .7, theta = 0)

# Define the output file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/02-population-spike-map-AU-power.png"

# Render the high-quality image
rayshader::render_highquality(
  filename = output_file,

  light = TRUE,
  lightdirection = 225,

```

The initial geometry plot and the raster plot are the same as above.

For the purpose of demonstration I have kept the Z-Scale consistent throughout these plots.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is `zscale` in rayshader?"}
In `rayshader`, the `zscale` parameter controls **how "tall" or "flat" the spikes appear** in the 3D render. It’s a scaling factor that translates data values (population, density, etc.) into vertical height, relative to the X-Y spacing of the matrix.

Think of it like a **height exaggeration dial**:

-   **Smaller `zscale` → taller spikes**
-   **Larger `zscale` → flatter terrain**

Internally: actual_z_height = value_in_matrix / zscale

This means if the largest value is 100, and I want the tallest spike to be 50 units high, the `zscale` should be `100 / 50 = 2`.

**Typical guidelines**: - Raw population data → try `zscale = 100–500` - Log-transformed data → try `zscale = 0.1–0.5` - Square root or power transforms → `zscale = 0.2–5`

Use `summary(as.vector(pop_mat_transformed))` to inspect the data range, then pick a `zscale` that gives a good spread of spike heights without distorting the map.

*Note: `zscale` only affects **height geometry**, not **color scaling**. So it’s often used in conjunction with a separate transformation or color map to fine-tune visual contrast.*
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How to Pick a Z-Scale (Sort Of Scientifically)" collapse="true"}
There’s no exact formula for `zscale`, but we *can* estimate a good starting point using our data summary.

The `zscale` is a **divisor**, so higher values flatten spikes, and lower values exaggerate them.

Some heuristics: - `zscale ≈ max(mat) / 100` if we want tallest spike ≈ 100 units - `zscale ≈ IQR(mat) / 10` to reveal top quartile structure - `zscale ≈ (max - median) / 10` for visual emphasis above the median

Ultimately, it depends on the story we want to tell:

If we want to emphasize major cities: Flatten the tails.\
If we want to reveal regional contrasts: Compress the top.
:::

Below are the results.

### Log Transformed

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
*Understanding Logarithmic Transformations*

A logarithmic transformation (e.g. ( \log\_{10}(x + 1) )) is a **strong compression** tool used when there are extreme outliers. It transforms multiplicative differences into additive ones—making very large values much smaller and **visually flattening** steep spikes.

However, in spike maps:

-   Log transformations **can overcorrect**, making even major cities appear flat.
-   You often need to set extremely low `zscale` values (e.g., 0.01) to see anything.
-   Regional variation may increase, but **overall visual impact is lost**.

This approach may be useful when your focus is on **low-population areas**, or if you want to **compare towns more evenly**, but it usually doesn’t preserve the dramatic effect that spike maps are designed to highlight.
:::

```         
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
    0.7     0.7     1.1     1.6     1.8     9.5 6615067 
```

Z-Scale = 0.25

### Square Root Transformation

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
*Understanding Square Root Transformations*

A square root transformation (i.e. ( \sqrt{x} ) or ( x\^{0.5} )) is a gentle way to compress large values and boost lower ones. It’s often used when data has a **right-skewed distribution**—like population density—where most values are small, but a few (major metro areas) are extremely large.

For population spike maps, applying a square root transformation helps:

-   Reduce the **height disparity** between capital cities and rural towns.
-   Reveal **regional contours** that would otherwise appear flat.
-   Preserve the **visual narrative** of population concentration while improving readability.

In practice, this is a good default when you want **subtle enhancement** without overwhelming changes to the data’s distribution.
:::

```         
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
    1.0     1.0     1.4     3.1     2.2   114.8 6615067 
```

Z-Scale = 0.25

### Power Transformation

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
*Understanding Power Transformations*

Power transformations apply an exponent ( \lambda ) to population values to reduce skew. When ( \lambda \< 1 ), high values (e.g. major cities) are compressed, while low values (regional centers) are gently lifted, allowing more visual differentiation across the density spectrum.

For this spike map, I used a ( x\^{0.7} ) transformation, which softens the dominance of ultra-dense metro areas without losing their height entirely. This revealed more mid-density variation across regional Australia, such as inland towns and coastal urban fringes.

This technique is a practical alternative to log transforms, which can over-flatten data.
:::

```         
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
    1.0     1.0     1.6     8.0     3.1   765.1 6615067 
```

Z-Scale = 0.25

### On Transforming the Data (or Not)

The power transformation seems to be the most effective at revealing the regional variation in population density while still maintaining the dramatic effect of the spike map. The log transformation, while useful for reducing extreme values, tends to flatten the map too much, making it less visually appealing. The square root transformation provides a middle ground but doesn't quite capture the same level of detail as the power transformation.

Australia’s population distribution is extreme. The vast majority of the continent is sparsely populated or completely uninhabited. Most people live in a few coastal cities, with Sydney and Melbourne absolutely dwarfing the rest. This isn’t a data error or an outlier problem, it’s the reality of Australia's population distribution. It's not a bug—it’s a feature. Statistically, this kind of data is heavily right-skewed. In other contexts, we might immediately opt for a log, square root, or even a Box-Cox transformation to normalize the distribution and make it more manageable. These are perfectly reasonable strategies when working with data that feeds into models, regressions, or any analysis where distributional assumptions matter. But in this context we're using the data for visual storytelling. The goal is not to minimize the skew, but to reveal it. The very thing that breaks our visualisations (the wild, vertical spike of Sydney) is essentially the entire point. It’s a visual cue for just how concentrated Australia's population is. Normalising that away risks flattening one of the most important takeaways from this visualisation. However, transforming the data can still be useful. We've seen that the the power transformation can make regional centres and smaller cities more visible, helping us avoid a sea of flatland with two impossible skyscrapers. But the trade off is that we are sacrifice relative contrast between the top end of the distribution. Sydney and Melbourne start to look more like Newcastle and Adelaide. There is no strictly “correct” answer in how to treat the population data, just different ways of framing the same data to tell different stories.

## From Raw Population to Population Density

Before diving deeper into tweaking spike maps, it's important to understand what the spike maps are actually showing, and how the choice of metric can dramatically affect what the final map communicates.

*How rayshader spike maps work*

When using `rayshader::plot_3d()` with a raster matrix (like population counts), each individual cell in the matrix is rendered as a tile on a 3D surface, with its height on the z-axis corresponding to the value in that tile.

Each tile represents a 400m x 400m square of land (0.16 km²), and the number in that tile is the raw population count for that square. So the "spikes" in the final map are simply how many people live in that specific 0.16 km² area. Tall spikes = high population count in a small fixed area — which, if you think about it, is also population density in disguise.

This means areas like the Sydney CBD, where thousands of people live in high-rise apartments stacked within just a few blocks, generate enormous vertical skyscrapers in the spike map. Suburbs like Parramatta, where people live in detached homes with yards, generate shorter, flatter spikes. And rural areas — vast tracts of land with very few people — barely rise off the ground.

*Why density still matters*

Even though each spike already reflects the number of people per 0.16 km² (i.e., density), that relationship is implicit. The raw values don't say "1,500 people per km²" — they just say "2400 people live here." So if you want to make comparisons with other datasets, interpret values directly, or rescale them using more sophisticated techniques (like power transformations), it can be useful to explicitly calculate population density by dividing the raw counts by the area.

More importantly, density as a concept shifts the visual narrative:

-   Raw population tells us how many people live somewhere.

-   Density tells us how tightly packed they are.

Consider two tiles that each contain 10,000 people:

-   One is an inner-city apartment block covering 0.16 km².

-   The other is a large, spread-out suburb spanning many square kilometres (i.e., across multiple tiles).

The raw population spikes may look similar. But in a density-based map, the city core explodes upward while the suburb flattens out — highlighting the intensity of urban living, not just raw headcount.

So, while rayshader’s tile-based spike map is already doing a kind of “visual density,” formalizing it helps with interpretation, flexibility, and cross-comparison — especially as we experiment with scaling, transformations, and thematic overlays.

```{r}
# Population Density Spike Map of Australia
# Setup: libraries, file paths, and projection — same as Section 1

get_population_data <- function() {
  pop_df <- sf::st_read(file_path) |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = crsAU)
  
  return(pop_df)
}

pop_sf <- get_population_data()

# Define file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/03-population-density-spike-map-AU_raw-population-points.png"

head(pop_sf)

# Save the plot
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pop_sf, color = "grey10", fill = "grey10") +
  theme_void() +  # or theme_classic() if you want axes
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )

ggsave(filename = output_file, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

### 3. SHP TO RASTER
### ----------------

bb <- sf::st_bbox(pop_sf)

get_raster_size <- function() {
  height <- sf::st_distance(
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymax"]]))
  )
  width <- sf::st_distance(
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymin"]]))
  )
  
  if (height > width) {
    height_ratio <- 1
    width_ratio <- width / height
  } else {
    width_ratio <- 1
    height_ratio <- height / width
  }
  
  return(list(width_ratio, height_ratio))
}
width_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[1]]
height_ratio <- get_raster_size()[[2]]

size <- 3000
width <- round((size * width_ratio), 0)
height <- round((size * height_ratio), 0)

get_population_raster <- function() {
  pop_rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
    pop_sf |>
      dplyr::select(population, geom),
    nx = width, ny = height
  )
  
  return(pop_rast)
}

pop_rast <- get_population_raster()

# Define output filename
output_file <- "outputs/images/03-population-density-spike-map-AU_raw-population-raster-preview.png"

# Open PNG device
png(filename = output_file, width = 2000, height = 1500, res = 300)

# Plot the raster
plot(pop_rast, main = "Population Raster", axes = FALSE, box = FALSE)

# Close the device
dev.off()

# Convert the stars object to a matrix for rayshader
pop_mat <- pop_rast |>
  as("Raster") |>
  rayshader::raster_to_matrix()

# Australian-themed colors
cols <- c(
  "#00843D", "#FFCD00", 
  "#FF8000", "#FF4500"
)

texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(cols)(2048)

# True Density transformation
# This is a more complex transformation that takes into account the density of points
# in the raster. It can be useful for visualizing population density.

# Calculate the density of points in the raster
cell_area_km2 <- 0.16
density_raster <- pop_mat / cell_area_km2 # Now we have density in people per km2

# Check the distribution of values to determine a reasonable Z scale
summary(as.vector(density_raster))

# Create the initial 3D object using the density raster
density_raster |>
  rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
  rayshader::plot_3d(
    heightmap = density_raster,
    solid = F,
    soliddepth = 0,
    zscale = 5,  # We need to play with this value with the transformed data
    shadowdepth = 0,
    shadow_darkness = .95,
    windowsize = c(800, 800),
    phi = 65,
    zoom = .65,
    theta = -30,
    background = "white"
  )

# Use this to adjust the view after building the window object
rayshader::render_camera(phi = 65, zoom = .4, theta = 0)

# Define the output file path
output_file <- "outputs/images/03-population-density-spike-map-AU.png"

# Render the high-quality image
rayshader::render_highquality(
  filename = output_file,
  preview = TRUE,
  light = TRUE,
  lightdirection = 225,
  lightaltitude = 60,
  lightintensity = 400,
  interactive = FALSE,
  width = width,
  height = height
)

# Close the 3D device
rgl::close3d()

```

## State Level Population Spike Maps

Next step was to create state level population spike maps. Australian state boundary data was downloaded from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

### **Understanding the Performance Bottleneck in Spatial Intersections**

The function that's taking hours to run is performing spatial intersections between Australian state boundaries and population data. Let me explain why this is computationally expensive:

#### **Primary Performance Bottlenecks**

1.  **`sf::st_intersection()` Complexity**: This spatial operation is computationally intensive because:

    -   It performs geometric overlay operations between two spatial datasets

    -   It checks for all points where geometries from both datasets intersect

    -   It computes new geometries representing these intersections

    -   It preserves attributes from both input datasets

2.  **Large Dataset Size**: This code is processing the Kontur population dataset for Australia:

    -   This dataset contains millions of polygons

    -   Each point/polygon has complex geometric properties requiring extensive calculations

    -   The operation must be repeated for each state boundary

3.  **Sequential Processing**: The `lapply()` function processes each state sequentially rather than in parallel, which doesn't leverage multi-core capabilities for this specific operation.

#### **Technical Explanation**

The spatial intersection algorithm must:

1.  Build spatial indices for both datasets

2.  Perform initial filtering using bounding boxes

3.  Calculate precise geometric intersections between potentially millions of polygons

4.  Create new geometries and copy attributes for all intersections

5.  Validate the topological integrity of resulting geometries

This involves many floating-point calculations, spatial index lookups, and memory operations.

#### **Optimization Possibilities**

To improve performance:

1.  Use spatial indexing pre-filtering (already built into sf, but can be configured)

2.  Simplify geometries before intersection to reduce computational complexity

3.  Break the problem into smaller geographic tiles and process in parallel

4.  Consider using specialized libraries like `lwgeom` for certain operations

5.  Implement parallel processing with `future` and `furrr` packages

The saveRDS approach is a practical workaround since the dataset isn't changing between runs.

```{r}
# Setup: libraries, file paths, and projection — same as Section 1

get_population_data <- function() {
  pop_df <- sf::st_read(file_path) |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = crsAU)
  
  return(pop_df)
}

pop_sf <- get_population_data()

# Load and transform Australian state boundaries
aus_states <- sf::st_read("data/boundaries/STE_2021_AUST_GDA2020.shp") |>
  sf::st_transform(crs = crsAU)

# Filter for the states/territories we want
filtered_states <- aus_states |>
  dplyr::filter(STE_NAME21 %in% c(
    "New South Wales", "Victoria", "Queensland", "South Australia",
    "Western Australia", "Tasmania", "Northern Territory", "Australian Capital Territory"
  ))

# Create a list of state geometries by name (using the filtered dataframe)
state_boundaries <- split(filtered_states, filtered_states$STE_NAME21)

# Create a named list of clipped population data per state
###### WARNING: This operation literally takes several hours to run
###### It is recommended to save the results after the first run, then comment out this function, and load the saved results for future tasks as required
###### There is likely a more efficient way to do this, but I haven't found it yet

state_pops <- lapply(state_boundaries, function(state_geom) {
  # Get the geometry column name for state_geom
  state_geom_col <- attr(state_geom, "sf_column")
  
  # Select only necessary columns from pop_sf
  pop_subset <- pop_sf %>% dplyr::select(population, geom)
  
  # Select only necessary columns from state_geom
  state_subset <- state_geom %>% dplyr::select(STE_NAME21, all_of(state_geom_col))
  
  #   # Perform intersection with reduced attributes
  sf::st_intersection(pop_subset, state_subset)
})

# IMPORTANT: Save the resulting list for future use (recommended)
saveRDS(state_pops, file = "data/processed/state_pops.rds")

# Later, we can reload with:
state_pops <- readRDS("data/processed/state_pops.rds")

#######################################################
#                 WORKING AREA FOR STATE SETTINGS
# Use this section to experiment with settings for
# individual states before using the modular approach
#######################################################

# Extract individual state population datasets
nsw_pop_sf <- state_pops[["New South Wales"]]
vic_pop_sf <- state_pops[["Victoria"]]
qld_pop_sf <- state_pops[["Queensland"]]
sa_pop_sf <- state_pops[["South Australia"]]
wa_pop_sf <- state_pops[["Western Australia"]]
tas_pop_sf <- state_pops[["Tasmania"]]
nt_pop_sf <- state_pops[["Northern Territory"]]
act_pop_sf <- state_pops[["Australian Capital Territory"]]

# Define custom aesthetic-inspired palette
cols <- c(
  "#f8f4e3",  # bone white
  "#fceea7",  # soft yellow
  "#f5c94c",  # mustard
  "#e67e22",  # burnt orange
  "#c0392b"   # rich red
)

# Create a smooth gradient texture
texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(cols)(1024)

# Process New South Wales
# ------------------------
# Get NSW bounding box
bb_nsw <- sf::st_bbox(nsw_pop_sf)

# Calculate dimensions
height_nsw <- sf::st_distance(
  sf::st_point(c(bb_nsw[["xmin"]], bb_nsw[["ymin"]])),
  sf::st_point(c(bb_nsw[["xmin"]], bb_nsw[["ymax"]]))
)
width_nsw <- sf::st_distance(
  sf::st_point(c(bb_nsw[["xmin"]], bb_nsw[["ymin"]])),
  sf::st_point(c(bb_nsw[["xmax"]], bb_nsw[["ymin"]]))
)

if (height_nsw > width_nsw) {
  height_ratio_nsw <- 1
  width_ratio_nsw <- width_nsw / height_nsw
} else {
  width_ratio_nsw <- 1
  height_ratio_nsw <- height_nsw / width_nsw
}

size <- 3000
width_nsw <- round((size * width_ratio_nsw), 0)
height_nsw <- round((size * height_ratio_nsw), 0)

# Generate raster for NSW
nsw_rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
  nsw_pop_sf |>
    dplyr::select(population, geom),
  nx = width_nsw, ny = height_nsw
)

# Convert to matrix
nsw_mat <- nsw_rast |>
  as("Raster") |>
  rayshader::raster_to_matrix()

# Create transformations for NSW
nsw_mat_log <- log10(nsw_mat + 1)  # +1 to avoid log(0)
nsw_mat_sqrt <- sqrt(nsw_mat)
nsw_mat_power <- nsw_mat^0.7


## --- START MODIFICATIONS ---
  
# Define parameters for landmass elevation and NA value handling
# base_elevation: How much to raise the entire NSW landmass.
# Adjust this value based on the scale of your nsw_mat population data.
# If population values are large, base_elevation might need to be larger.
# This value is in the same units as your nsw_mat data before zscale.
base_elevation <- 50.0  # Example: raise landmass by 50 units
epsilon <- 0.1          # Tiny offset to distinguish pop=0 from NA

# Create a definitive mask for the NSW state boundary
# This uses the nsw_rast as a template for grid alignment
nsw_boundary_sf <- state_boundaries[["New South Wales"]] # Assuming state_boundaries is loaded
template_stars_nsw <- nsw_rast # nsw_rast is the stars object from which nsw_mat was derived

nsw_definitive_boundary_rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
  nsw_boundary_sf,
  template = template_stars_nsw
)
nsw_definitive_mask_matrix_raw <- as(nsw_definitive_boundary_rast, "Raster")
nsw_definitive_mask_matrix <- rayshader::raster_to_matrix(nsw_definitive_mask_matrix_raw)
is_within_nsw_matrix <- !is.na(nsw_definitive_mask_matrix)

# Prepare the final height matrix for rendering
nsw_mat_final <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = nrow(nsw_mat), ncol = ncol(nsw_mat))

for (r in 1:nrow(nsw_mat)) {
  for (c in 1:ncol(nsw_mat)) {
    if (is_within_nsw_matrix[r, c]) { # If the cell is within NSW boundary
      if (!is.na(nsw_mat[r, c])) { # If there's population data
        # Add population data on top of base_elevation, plus epsilon
        nsw_mat_final[r, c] <- base_elevation + nsw_mat[r, c] + epsilon
      } else { # If it's NA within NSW (e.g., a lake, no data area)
        # Set to base_elevation, will be colored bone white
        nsw_mat_final[r, c] <- base_elevation
      }
    } else { # Outside NSW boundary
      nsw_mat_final[r, c] <- NA_real_
    }
  }
}

# NSW visualization settings (phi, theta, zoom might need tweaking with the new base height)
nsw_zscale <- 10        # Adjust as needed
nsw_phi <- 60           # Elevation angle
nsw_theta <- 25        # Azimuth angle
nsw_zoom <- 0.60        # Zoom level

# The existing 'texture' variable should work well with this new height scheme:
# Bone white for base_elevation (NA-within-NSW)

nsw_mat_final |>

  rayshader::plot_3d(
    heightmap = nsw_mat_final, 
    solid = TRUE,             
    soliddepth = -150,        
    zscale = nsw_zscale, # zscale scales the model here
    shadowdepth = 0,          
    shadow_darkness = .95,
    windowsize = c(800, 800),
    phi = nsw_phi,       # Initial RGL window phi
    zoom = nsw_zoom,     # Initial RGL window zoom

    background = "grey10"
  )

# Adjust view - Remember to go back and update the camera settings for the state variables above interactively - modify values as needed

# Define the output file path

#######################################################
#                 MODULAR APPROACH BELOW
# Once we've determined the best settings above,
# we can use them in the modular functions below
#######################################################

# Function to process state data and create matrices
process_state_data <- function(state_pop_sf, state_name, base_size = 3000) {
  # Get state bounding box
  bb <- sf::st_bbox(state_pop_sf)
  
  # Calculate dimensions
  height <- sf::st_distance(
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymax"]]))
  )
  width <- sf::st_distance(
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmin"]], bb[["ymin"]])),
    sf::st_point(c(bb[["xmax"]], bb[["ymin"]]))
  )
  
  if (height > width) {
    height_ratio <- 1
    width_ratio <- width / height
  } else {
    width_ratio <- 1
    height_ratio <- height / width
  }
  
  size <- base_size
  width <- round((size * width_ratio), 0)
  height <- round((size * height_ratio), 0)
  
  # Generate raster for the state
  rast <- stars::st_rasterize(
    state_pop_sf |>
      dplyr::select(population, geom),
    nx = width, ny = height
  )
  
  # Convert to matrix
  mat <- rast |>
    as("Raster") |>
    rayshader::raster_to_matrix()
  
  # Create transformations
  mat_log <- log10(mat + 1)  # +1 to avoid log(0)
  mat_sqrt <- sqrt(mat)
  mat_power <- mat^0.7
  
  return(list(
    mat = mat,
    mat_log = mat_log,
    mat_sqrt = mat_sqrt,
    mat_power = mat_power,
    width = width,
    height = height
  ))
}

# Function to create and save a 3D visualization for a state
visualize_state <- function(state_data, state_name, transformation = "log", 
                            output_dir = "outputs/images", preview = TRUE) {
  # Extract the correct matrix based on transformation type
  if (transformation == "log") {
    heightmap <- state_data$mat_log
  } else if (transformation == "sqrt") {
    heightmap <- state_data$mat_sqrt
  } else {
    heightmap <- state_data$mat_power
  }
  
  # Create the 3D object
  heightmap |>
    rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |>
    rayshader::plot_3d(
      heightmap = heightmap,
      solid = FALSE,
      soliddepth = 0,
      zscale = 10,  # Adjust as needed
      shadowdepth = 0,
      shadow_darkness = .95,
      windowsize = c(800, 800),
      phi = 65,     # Elevation angle
      zoom = 0.65,  # Zoom level
      theta = -30,  # Azimuth angle
      background = "white"
    )
  
  # Adjust view - Remember to go back and update the camera settings for the state variables above interactively - modify values as needed
  rayshader::render_camera(phi = 75, zoom = 0.7, theta = 0)
  
  # Define the output file path
  output_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0("04-state-population-spike-map-", gsub(" ", "-", state_name), ".png"))
  
  # Render the high-quality image
  rayshader::render_highquality(
    filename = output_file,
    preview = preview,
    light = TRUE,
    lightdirection = 225,
    lightaltitude = 60,
    lightintensity = 400,
    interactive = FALSE,
    width = state_data$width,
    height = state_data$height
  )
}

# Process all states
state_names <- c("New South Wales", "Victoria", "Queensland", "South Australia",
                 "Western Australia", "Tasmania", "Northern Territory", "Australian Capital Territory")

# Initialize a list to store state data
all_states_data <- list()

# Loop through each state, process the data, and visualize
for (state_name in state_names) {
  # Extract the state population sf object
  state_pop_sf <- state_pops[[state_name]]
  
  # Process the state data
  state_data <- process_state_data(state_pop_sf, state_name)
  
  # Save to list
  all_states_data[[state_name]] <- state_data
  
  # Visualize and save the spike map (using log transformation as default)
  visualize_state(state_data, state_name, transformation = "log")
}

# When done with all visualizations, close the window
rgl::close3d()
```

## Cracking the Landmass and Background Rendering.

Goal: Create a high-fidelity spike map of NSW using rayshader, with a clean dark background, a bone-white landmass, and population spikes in a glowing gradient — all rendered as a solid 3D slab like a geographic slice of marble.

The Challenge: Why is My Background Not Changing?

The initial challenge was deceptively simple: just change the background color.

I started by trying to set the background parameter in rayshader::plot_3d(). It looked like it worked — the RGL preview window showed the grey background just fine. But when I ran render_highquality(), every single image exported came out with the same default pale grey backdrop.

I tried: - Setting background = "grey10" in plot_3d() - Using hex codes (#1A1A1A) in both plot_3d() and render_highquality() - Playing with backgroundhigh and backgroundlow parameters in render_highquality() - Changing light, ambient light, sample count — everything short of ritual sacrifice

Nothing stuck. I kept seeing the same washed-out renders. It became clear: plot_3d’s background only affects the preview window. The rendered image is built independently by rayrender, not rgl, so the backdrop is a whole different beast.

The Fix: Use ground_material

The fix was hilariously simple, but well-hidden: the background in render_highquality() is controlled by the plane beneath the scene, and unless you tell it otherwise, it renders in a default material that ignores your color.

The solution: ground_material = rayrender::diffuse(color = "#1A1A1A")

This one line made everything click — the background was finally actually dark grey.

Masking the Landmass

With the background fixed, my next aesthetic goal was to give the landmass of NSW a clean, uniform elevation (like a plateau), while still letting population spikes protrude upward. And critically — unpopulated but valid areas (e.g., lakes, parks, no-data regions) needed to be colored bone white, while populated pixels moved into the yellow→orange→red gradient.

To achieve this, I: 1. Created a raster mask of the NSW geometry using st_rasterize() and aligned it to the same grid as the population matrix. 2. Wrote a custom loop to build a new height matrix (nsw_mat_final) that: - Assigned a constant base elevation to all in-boundary cells - Added a small epsilon (1 unit) to cells with population, to shift them into a different color bucket - Left out-of-bound cells as NA so they’d render transparent

Result: A raised landmass with subtle elevation, and actual population data starting just above it.

Adding Depth: Extruding the Landmass

To complete the slab-of-marble effect, I wanted the map to look like it had been cut out of something. Luckily, rayshader::plot_3d() has a solid = TRUE mode that turns your matrix into a volumetric chunk.

With the landmass raised to a base of 750 units, I used: solid = TRUE, soliddepth = -300,

This extruded the map downward, making it feel grounded and physical. The whole thing now looks like a sculpted tile, with spikes jutting from a clean top surface.

Final Thoughts

This was a weirdly gnarly part of the project. I spent hours adjusting parameters that didn’t matter because the rendering logic between plot_3d() and render_highquality() is split across two worlds (rgl and rayrender), and the docs didn’t always make this clear.

Background rendering works, landmass masking works, and the slab depth adds a satisfying weight to the final render.

Next up: fine-tuning the camera position (it’s tricky to center landmasses in 3D space), and then generating maps for the other states.

### The Scale Mismatch Problem (and the spike_scale fix)

The base elevation strategy worked visually, but created a subtle problem that only became obvious later when moving to a Windows machine and regenerating the maps: the spikes had disappeared.

The cause was a scale mismatch between `base_elevation` and the log-transformed population values. The log10 transform of population data produces values roughly in the range 0–5 (log10(100,000) ≈ 5). But `base_elevation` was set to 50 — ten times larger. When you build the height matrix as `base_elevation + log10(population + 1)`, the result ranges from 50 to about 54.7. The spikes are real, but they’re only a 9% variation sitting on top of a giant platform. At any normal camera angle and zscale, they’re invisible.

The original code (before the base_elevation refactor) didn’t have this problem because it had no base platform at all — the height matrix was just `log10(population + 1)`, ranging from 0 to ~5, and the spikes occupied the full height range.

The fix was to introduce a `spike_scale` multiplier that’s applied to the log-transformed population before the base elevation is added:

```r
log_pop <- log10(pop_mat + 1) * spike_scale
final_mat[within] <- base_elevation + log_pop[within]
```

With `spike_scale = 10`, the spike heights reach up to ~47 units above the base of 50 — roughly equal in magnitude, which gives the platform enough visual weight to be clear at full zoom-out while the spikes are still prominent. Both parameters can now be tuned independently per state.

## Per-State Camera Tuning

One thing that became obvious pretty quickly when rendering state maps: there is no universal camera angle.

Australia’s states and territories vary enormously — not just in size, but in shape and orientation. Western Australia is a wide, roughly rectangular block. Queensland stretches diagonally and is dominated by coastal population hugging the southeast corner. The Northern Territory is tall and sparse. The ACT is tiny, dense, and almost circular. Tasmania is an island sitting below a vast ocean of empty space. What looks good for Victoria — compact, roughly rectangular, population concentrated in the south — looks completely wrong for a state like WA, where you’re zoomed out so far that Melbourne-sized cities would disappear.

The camera parameters that matter are:

- **phi** — the elevation angle (how high above the scene you’re looking from)
- **theta** — the azimuth rotation (which direction you’re facing)
- **zoom** — how close or far the camera sits
- **zscale** — vertical exaggeration of the spikes (lower = taller spikes)

Each of these needs to be dialled in per state. Getting the right combination is iterative — you set some values, look at the result, adjust, repeat.

To handle this properly I built a dedicated tuning script (`R/03_tune_camera.R`). The workflow is:

1. Set `tune_state` at the top of the script to whichever state you want to work on
2. Run through the script line by line in RStudio — it processes the state matrix at a reduced resolution (1000px vs the 3000px used in final renders, so it’s faster) and opens a 3D preview
3. In the tuning loop (Section 7), edit `tune_phi`, `tune_theta`, and `tune_zoom`, then re-run that block — it updates the camera and saves a quick snapshot to `outputs/tuning_preview.png`
4. When happy, call `print_settings()` in the console — it outputs a ready-to-paste entry for the `state_settings` list in `02_render_maps.R`

The separation between tuning and rendering keeps the batch script clean. Script 2 just reads the dialled-in settings and runs, no interactive fiddling required.

## macOS Compatibility

Worth noting for anyone trying to run this on macOS: the interactive rgl preview window — which is the natural environment for camera tuning in rayshader — does not work on macOS 26 Tahoe. It barely works on earlier versions.

Here’s what happened when I tried to set this up on a MacBook running macOS 26.0.1.

**Without XQuartz installed**, rgl fails to load entirely:

```
Error: unable to load shared object ‘rgl.so’:
  Library not loaded: /opt/X11/lib/libGLU.1.dylib
```

rgl’s compiled binary links against `libGLU`, which lives inside XQuartz. No XQuartz, no rgl.

**With XQuartz installed**, rgl loads, but the window fails to open:

```
X11 error: GLXBadContext
Error in rgl::open3d(...): open failed
```

GLX is the OpenGL extension for X11. macOS 26 dropped native OpenGL support, so even with XQuartz present, the OpenGL context can’t be created and the window never appears. rgl even prints a warning about this explicitly in newer versions.

The good news: `render_highquality()` is unaffected. It uses rayrender under the hood, which is a pure CPU-based path tracer — no OpenGL, no rgl window, no display required. Final renders work fine on macOS.

For camera tuning on macOS, the workaround is to use the null device with `render_snapshot()`:

```r
options(rgl.useNULL = TRUE)
# ... plot_3d() ...
render_camera(phi = 65, theta = 0, zoom = 0.70)
render_snapshot("outputs/tuning_preview.png")
```

This renders offscreen and saves a fast (non-raytraced) PNG you can inspect. It’s less immediate than dragging a live window, but it works. The tuning script (`03_tune_camera.R`) is structured around this approach.

If you want a proper interactive window, a Linux or Windows machine with working OpenGL is the path of least resistance.

## Blender Pipeline

The Blender export pipeline was partially successful. Several file formats exported cleanly from R, but the format that works best natively in Blender — the one with full material and geometry support — failed to render. I ended up with a 3D object I could rotate and inspect, but couldn’t meaningfully manipulate: no ability to animate spike growth, adjust materials, or work with the geometry dynamically. The ceiling was hit pretty quickly.

If the goal is a cinematic, animated spike map, the better approach is to build it natively in Blender from scratch rather than exporting from rayshader. Blender also has the significant advantage of CUDA acceleration, which would make rendering considerably faster than rayshader’s CPU-bound pipeline.

Where rayshader shines is that Rayshader maps are honest in a way Blender renders aren’t: the data transformation is explicit, the code is open, and someone can audit exactly how the spikes were generated. Blender gives you full creative control over lighting, camera, and materials — but that same freedom means the final image is harder to verify. One is data visualisation, the other is closer to data art.

A future project is to rebuild the same maps natively in Blender and compare the two workflows — the reproducibility and auditability of the R approach against the creative range and rendering power of Blender.
